detail: The Greek Sea Peoples did not come from outside and wreck Greece. They are what remains of the Mycenaean palaces' own sea-power. In the palaces' last years each wanax called up rowers and posted coastguards along the shore. The Drought then cut the grain, and trade shrank under drought and raiding together, so the ration system could no longer pay the fleets in grain and bronze. The crews kept the ships and carried on the raiding that palaces had always done on the side, against Anatolian and Cypriot coasts for goods and captive women, but now for themselves. In 1160 the palace fires are about forty years in the past. (Divergence: historically the Sea Peoples were a mixed coalition, and no Aegean destruction can be firmly pinned on them.)

Leadership among the raiders passed to small men: former local headmen (qa-si-re-u), who were palace officials and never kings, and ship-captains. Rank is counted in hulls and oars, so a fifty-oar galley is a warband of fifty. Each lord holds a piece of ruined palace and calls himself king, claiming a throne he never held in a system that no longer exists. By 1160 the Naue II sword marks a warrior caste. Lords fight one another freely, and their alliances last only as long as a shared enemy does.

The few Mycenaean palaces still standing in 1160, Mycenae, Tiryns and Athens, survive because their lords brought their springs or cisterns inside the walls during the Drought. These cistern kings rule by controlling water. They let it out to client villages, keep young warbands loyal with drink and plunder, and drive out anyone they cannot feed. Everyone outside the walls becomes a raider: cast-out retainers, starving herders, and villages fleeing the Cyclopes. The landless bands serve the cistern kings, raid them, and dream of taking their walls. The two groups need each other and hate each other.

The cistern kings learned how to build their walled water-works from the Cyclopes. Other ties between the cistern kings and the Cyclopes are not yet settled. Cyclopes driven down from their caves by the Drought are one source of the landless raiding bands, because villages flee before them.

In 1160 Mycenae still stands as a cistern king's citadel and has not yet burned. Its first burning is to come as the Drought deepens, and the story will decide its cause (rival ship-lords, Cyclopes or the Drought's beasts). (Divergence: historically the Mycenae citadel burned c. 1200–1180 and again c. 1150/1125.)

In 1160 Greece has begun its descent into a dark age. Potters still paint warships and warriors on the march, the same pictorial peak that produced the Lefkandi griffin vessel. As the Drought deepens, what remains fails in a wave of destructions. Jon's road runs through a Greece that is sliding faster and faster into a true dark age.

In 1160 the most valuable plunder is people. Raiders take women and children for labour or ransom and sell them on to Cyprus or the Levant. The trade was inherited from the palaces, which already took people as plunder (the Pylos 'war-captives').

Coastal villagers across Greece and the islands have moved uphill into fortified peak villages, such as Karphi and Kastri on Crete and the upland refuge villages of Mount Ida. The landscape reads as empty shores and crowded hilltops. Refuge communities distrust any armed band that arrives from the sea.

Greek oral tradition counts the failed invasions of Egypt, which ended in Ramesses III's Year 8 victory (~1177), among its great wars, followed by bad homecomings. Survivors found their palaces burned or seized and their granaries empty. Turned away, they became landless ship-lords, and their sons raid because their fathers could not go home. Raider bards sing of the Delta the way Odysseus lies about it: plunder first, then Pharaoh's terrible counterstroke. (Divergence: there is no historical evidence of a Greek epic about invading Egypt.)
Troy exists in this world. Greek memory holds both Troy and the southern wars against Egypt as great wars.

Ramesses III is the villain of the Greek raiders' poems about the Delta war, just as they are the bound captives on his temple walls. His Year 8 victory over the Sea Peoples falls around 1177, about 17 years before the story. In Egypt the war is remembered as a defeat of northern invaders won at great cost, and the nobility still resents paying for it.

Overrides prehistory: the original Sherden came from Sardinia, not Greece, and have no connection to the Greek Sea Peoples. The two are separate peoples. The modern Sherden keep no connection overseas and have no kinship with the Greek raiders. Ordinary Egyptians nonetheless lump the Sherden and the Greek raiders together as the same 'foreign invader' type. (Divergence: historically the Sherden appear in Egyptian lists alongside the other Sea Peoples, and their origin is uncertain, possibly Sardinian.)

The Drought is the driving cause of the Greek collapse. It cut the grain that fed the palace ration system, and with trade also shrinking, the palaces could no longer pay their fleets. It drives the Cyclopes down from their caves, swells the landless raiding bands, and later topples the rally of the surviving citadels. (Divergence: historically drought was one factor among many, and the Aegean evidence for it is thin.)
How and why did Ramesses II come to recruit Sardinian warriors as the first Sherden, and how did the corps come to lose every tie overseas?
Does any warlord still claim the old title wanax, or has "king" sunk to the headman's word?
Which citadels still stand in 1160, and is Mycenae one of them?
Who buys captives in 1160: Cyprus, Tyre, Egypt, or all three?
How do Troy and the southern wars relate in Greek memory: one cycle of songs, or separate ages?
After the Year 8 victory, did Ramesses III kill, enslave or settle the captured Greeks, and are any of them living in Egypt now?
Beyond the water-works, what other ties bind the cistern kings to the Cyclopes?
How do Greek raiders see the Sherden: as fellow foreigners in Pharaoh's pay, or as strangers with no meaning to them?
Did Greeks who served Hatti as mercenaries come home after Hattusa fell, or do some remain in Anatolia?
On Jon's road, refuge villages that fear anything arriving from the sea see a band in Sherden horned helmets and bar their gates. His first fight in Greece is to be let in.
Jon hears his father sung as the villain of the Delta war, perhaps in the same season he learns, or will learn, that Ramesses III is dead.
The Cyclopes taught the water-works. As the Drought drives them down, they come back for the springs.
Jon's exodus inverts Year 8: the son of the pharaoh who threw the Greeks back leads Greek refugees to shelter in Egypt.
At Pi-Ramesses, the habit of lumping the Sherden with the raiders becomes a political weapon. The nobles or Tiye's faction use it to make the guard look foreign at the moment of the coup.
The captive trade flows into Cyprus, the island that houses the purple guild, which raises the question of where the guild's own servants come from.
With Tyre at war with Assyria after the coup, Tyre's merchant-royals swallow their disgust and hire Greek ship-lords as rowers and marines.
